old: where the nymphs weave their sea-purple robes—a wondrous sight to see—and fresh water always flows within.

old: so people wouldn’t know of his arrival, and so she could tell him everything without his wife, fellow citizens, or friends recognizing him until he had taken revenge on the wicked suitors.

Splitting the two purposes into separate sentences keeps the same information but is easier to follow by ear.

"Vassal" carries strong medieval-feudal connotations that can feel out of place and may not register clearly with a general listener; "his man" (a subordinate follower) conveys the same relationship in plain language.

"Beechmast" (the fallen nuts of beech trees, used as pig feed) is an obscure term almost no general listener will recognize, and nothing in the sentence clarifies it. "Beech nuts" is the same food in ordinary vocabulary.

"Undressed" here means untanned/untreated, but a listener will default to the everyday sense of "undressed" (unclothed), producing a confusing image right next to "as an outer garment." "Raw deerskin" gives the same meaning without the collision.
